title: Lines and movement — Image Wiki
text:
Lines and movement
  A line in a picture is hardly ever drawn. It is an edge, an alignment, a gaze or a trajectory — and its job is to give the eye a direction to travel in and a speed to travel at.

  
    Termline / visual movement
    Also calledleading lines, implied lines, sight lines, visual direction, eye path
    Not the same asoutline, motion blur, rhythm, visual hierarchy
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        What lines doThe honest version of leading linesWhy the diagonal is the fastest directionMovement nobody drawsCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Find a photograph with a road in it. Before you have decided anything about the picture, your eye has already run up the road. Nobody drew a line there. It is two verges and a bit of tarmac, and you followed it anyway.
Getty's definition is the useful one: a line is the path made by a point moving in space, and lines are what most often mark the edges of a form (SRC-001). Notice that the definition never mentions ink. In a photograph nothing is outlined, and yet the frame is full of lines:

An edge between two areas — a roofline, a shoreline, a shadow's boundary, a table's rim.
An alignment — three windows, a row of heads, footprints in snow. Separate things your eye joins up because they nearly fall on a path (Gestalt grouping).
A gaze — the invisible segment from an eye to whatever it is looking at.
A gesture — a pointing finger, an outstretched arm, the lean of a body.
A trajectory — the space a moving thing is heading into, which reads as a line before anything has moved.

Photography Life's list of what makes a line in practice runs from roads and rivers to rainbows, the Milky Way, hard-edged shadows and "the shape of people" (SRC-020). If two parts of a picture are connected, something is doing the connecting.
What lines do
They lead. Getty files this under movement: the path the eye takes through a work, directed along lines, edges, shapes and colour (SRC-002).
They divide. This is the half people forget, and Photography Life states it exactly: the eye flows along a line easily and across it with difficulty (SRC-020). A horizon through the middle is not neutral, it is a wall. A fence, a kerb, a shadow's edge, a railing — each one splits the frame into a side you are on and a side you are not. The fix is not to remove the line but to break it: the same writer looks for soft horizons, or for something that crosses from sky to land — a cloud, a rainbow, a lightning bolt, a tree — so that the two halves are stitched rather than stacked (SRC-020). A barrier used deliberately is how you keep the eye in: a wall of foliage at the border closes a composition instead of decorating it.
They set a direction and a speed. Horizontal reads as rest, because things lying parallel to the ground are at rest. Vertical reads as height and formality. Diagonal reads as movement, because a thing at an angle is either falling or already going (SRC-001, SRC-030).


Horizontals: Vernet, A Calm at a Mediterranean Port, 1770
Diagonals: Vernet, Storm with a Shipwreck, 1754


Claude-Joseph Vernet, A Calm at a Mediterranean Port, 1770, and Storm with a Shipwreck, 1754. Both public domain. Getty uses this same pair to teach horizontal and diagonal line.
One painter, one subject — a coast with a ship and some figures — and opposite dominant directions.
In the calm, list the horizontals: the sea's flat edge, the top of the harbour wall, the quay's coping, the stacked lengths of timber in the foreground, the reflected sun lying flat on the water. The only strong verticals are the lighthouse and the ship's masts, and both stand square. Nothing in the geometry is going anywhere.
In the storm, almost nothing is level. The wrecked ship's masts and yards make a bundle of crossing diagonals, the wave crests run up to the left, the shafts of rain slant, the great rock is a wedge, the men hauling on the rope lean into a diagonal of their own. The one thing standing upright is the tower on the right, and it reads as the only safe object in the picture.


The honest version of leading lines

Arrives somewherethe track ends at the barnthe eye is deliveredArrives nowherethe same track, aimed at empty fieldthe eye is dropped in a blank patchLeads outthe same track, aimed past the borderthe eye leaves the picture and does not come back

The track has the same shape and the same starting width in all three panels, and the barn sits in the same place. The only variable is where the track is aimed.
Arrives: the line delivers you to the barn, and the composition closes. Arrives nowhere: the identical line drops you on a blank patch of field, and the barn — still there, still the subject — now has to be found without help. Leads out: the line takes your eye through the right-hand border, and there is nothing beyond the border to come back for.
A line does not lead because it is a line. It leads to wherever it points, which is only useful if something is there.


Photography Life makes the point against its own tradition, with a pair of the author's own photographs: the version with a fallen log in the foreground as a leading line is "actually quite distracting", and the simpler version without it is stronger (SRC-020). The advice that follows is the right test — find the line, work out how much attention it draws, then ask whether the picture benefits from a connection at all.



Alfred Stieglitz, The Steerage, 1907 (Google Art Project). Public domain.
One line doing both jobs at once. The pale gangway runs from the lower left up to the right — the lightest, straightest, longest shape in the picture, and a diagonal.
As a divider it is absolute. The people above it and the people below it never mix; the frame is two populations, and that division is what the photograph is about.
As a link it is also the route across. Your eye gets from the lower deck to the upper one by running up it, and it makes the trip in one movement. Notice the bracing around it: the funnel at the left is a hard vertical, the ladder at the right a counter-diagonal offering a second and much slower way between the levels, and the sagging chains of the railing repeat the gangway's angle in miniature.


Why the diagonal is the fastest direction
A rectangle has two directions built into it, and every horizontal or vertical in the picture is parallel to one of the four edges — it lines up with the frame and settles. A diagonal is parallel to nothing. It is the only direction that never agrees with the border it lives in, which is why it will not sit still: design writing reports diagonals as carrying the most visual weight and suggesting movement and action (SRC-030), and Cooper Hewitt lists activate the diagonal among the fourteen things a poster can do — diagonals cut across the surface and drive into its depth (POST-001-SUP1).



Albrecht Dürer, The Four Horsemen, from The Apocalypse, 1498, woodcut (National Gallery of Art, CC0).
Every mark here is a line, which makes it the clearest possible demonstration. Smarthistory's observation about the hat on one of the horsemen is worth stopping on: it is made of a few black contour strokes, and there is no hat there at all — only marks on paper that your eye agrees to treat as one (SRC-007).
Now count the directions. All four horses face right and the group drives left to right; their forelegs, the riders' bodies, the raised sword, the bow, the flying reins and the scales all repeat a bank of roughly parallel diagonals. The background is ruled with plain horizontal lines that shade the sheet and, at the same time, read as the ground streaming past.
The exception proves the rule. At the lower left the pit of hell and the bishop being swallowed are drawn in dense curls going nowhere, and that corner is the only part of the picture that feels stationary — because it is the only part with no diagonal in it.


Movement nobody draws



Leonardo da Vinci, The Virgin of the Rocks, c. 1483–86 (Musée du Louvre). Public domain.
Follow the eyes and the hands, in order. The angel on the right looks out of the picture at you, and points across it to the infant John on the left. John kneels with his hands together toward the infant Christ. Christ raises a hand back at him. Mary looks down at Christ, her right hand on John's shoulder and her left hovering above her son's head.
That is a closed circuit made of nothing. Smarthistory calls these sight lines and describes the effect precisely: you enter through the angel's gaze and are then locked into a cycle of movement between the figures (SRC-007). Not one of those lines exists as a mark on the panel, and they are the strongest structure in it.


Two more implied lines are worth naming because they decide ordinary pictures. Gaze works even when you cannot see the face — a head turned away still points. And the space in front of a moving subject is read as its path, which is why a runner with room ahead is running and the same runner cropped against the leading border is stopped.
Common mistakes

"A leading line makes a composition stronger." It makes a route. If the route ends in nothing, or leaves the frame, you have built a slide out of the picture.
"Lines have to be straight." A curve is a line with a changing direction, and it reads slower and softer for exactly that reason (SRC-001).
"Diagonals are dynamic, so tilt the camera." Tilting makes every horizontal and vertical in the scene into a near-diagonal at once, which reads as unease rather than motion — that is what a Dutch angle is for.
"A horizon is just where the sky stops." It is the longest line in most landscapes and the strongest divider in the frame. Where you put it decides which half the picture is about (The rule of thirds).
"Implied lines are a metaphor." They are as effective as painted ones and often more so. A gaze can beat a road.


Reading the lines in an image

Squint and name the two or three strongest lines. Include edges, alignments and gazes, not just objects that look like lines.
Say the dominant direction out loud: horizontal, vertical or diagonal. That is most of the picture's mood.
Follow each line to its end. Does it arrive at something, stop at nothing, or leave through a border?
Find the barriers. Is anything cutting the frame into parts the eye cannot cross?
If something in the picture is moving or looking, check whether there is room in front of it.
